title: Line of Sight
subtitle: A survey of the Harrow chain
story:
The villages of the Harrows are built where they are for one reason: glimstones, which come down with the melt and settle on the river banks. By day the glimstones look like ordinary pebbles. When the sun goes down, they glow like the precious stones they are, so the villagers gather them at night.

But on some nights the meltwater surges down the valleys too, and anyone out on the banks can be swept away. To warn the gatherers on those nights, a network of beacon towers was built across the mountain range. You are the warden of that network. Your work is knowing which towers can see which villages, and which fires must burn so that no village goes unwarned. Walk the ridges, solve the puzzles, and work out which beacons to light before the water rises.

done.title: Dispatch analysis complete!
done.body: Interesting: even though the Crown is the busiest station, it is not the one that connects the whole network. That job hangs on just a small station with little traffic. You fold the ledgers away. The light is fading, and there is a sound off the head of the valley that was not there this morning. The water is rushing down! Choose which four beacons to light so that everyone is aware of the danger!

escapeDone.title: The chain is lit
escapeDone.body: You put the torch to the Crown's brazier — not a warning, an order — and away below, one after another, the towers answer it. The Ladder takes the light, then the Hood, then the Spindle, and last, far down the ridge where you would never have thought to put a fire, the Broken Tooth. Below, no one goes out to the rock banks. On any other warm night in the year they would be scattered with lamps and quiet voices and the cold shine of a good take. Tonight there is only the river, getting louder. Good work keeping everyone safe!

debrief.title: How the Harrows worked
debrief.intro: This world was built to argue one thing: that importance is not a quantity a node has, but a property of what a set of them covers. You met the claim twice, on two different networks over the same ground — once on paper, in a book of dispatches, and once by eye, on a range where the only record of what can see what is the walking you did yourself.

_designNotes.rooms:
Designed 2026-09-02. TWELVE rooms, OPEN-WORLD per canon (all doors direction:'open', every room unlockedWhen:true); puzzle ORDER is enforced on the hotspots via availableWhen + lockedBody, never by closed doors. Why open-world here specifically: the escape rewards roaming, because the survey is nine separate spyglass pickups and the player should be free to gather them in any order and revisit.
WHY NINE TOWER ROOMS. Each lightable tower needs its own room because a tower's line-tile records which villages IT overlooks, and that can only be judged by standing on it. Nine is also the brute-force floor (C(9,4)=126) and the count the placement is VERIFIED at — cutting one to save art means re-running place_coverage.py and re-verifying, not just deleting a room.
ARC IS SPATIAL, NOT TEMPORAL, per canon: an open world cannot bake a time-of-day arc per room without shipping a backtracking player into the past. Every scene bakes its place-constant character (bright high-altitude day) and the ONE clock — day to night — is a global state variant fired when the ninth line-tile lands. Every room therefore needs a night variant: one unmasked edit of its base, never an edit of an edit.
LOOK DEVIATES FROM THE CORPUS HOUSE STYLE ON PURPOSE. The usual dusk / teal-and-amber does not apply: beacons claimed HIGH-KEY DAYLIGHT in notes/vibe_inventory.md, and the physics needs it (smoke must read against blue; sun charges the glimstone and swells the tarn). Do not let generation drift warm.
SPECTACLE ROOMS: Whistlegate (boss) and the Crown (escape payoff), per the standing rule. The Crown is the richest — it is the only place the whole chain is visible at once, which is the reason the finale can exist there.
ambient is 'dust' — the vocabulary is a CLOSED SET (fireflies/snow/embers/leaves/dust/rays/none) and anything else silently falls through to fireflies. Intent: wind-blown grit and spindrift off the tops.
_designNotes.worldPlate: Rewritten 2026-09-02 (twice). The plate is a brilliant CLEAR-SKY DAY: snow and glacier must be visible because the escape's danger is a moraine-dammed lake fed by the day's melt, and the sky must be clear because signalling by day is SMOKE and a grey column is invisible against grey cloud. The earlier 'flat overcast, shadowless' version also collided with modeling/canal's claim in notes/vibe_inventory.md; beacons' own claim is HIGH-KEY DAYLIGHT, which means hard sun. THE GLIMSTONE IS DELIBERATELY NOT GLOWING HERE — by day it is a basket of dull grey pebbles, and the negative prompt says 'no glowing or luminous objects' to stop the model reaching for it. The islands carry the WORKINGS instead (cleared plots, windbreaks, baskets, drying racks, wading stakes), which says the valley is used at night without spending the night image. The one night image in the whole scenario is the four beacons burning with the answering village lamps below — do not spend it here, and do not let the day scenes drift warm or amber. Terrain is Khan Tengri elevation repainted (notes.md -> The range): the landforms are real.
_designNotes.cover: THREE fires, not four — the thumbnail must not hand over the escape's answer count. The fires are small and distant; the frame is a bright day, so the warm note reads as precious rather than ambient.
_designNotes.theStones: GLIMSTONE (Lucas, 2026-09-02) — the reason the villages exist and the reason anyone is in the valley at night. It is PERSISTENT LUMINESCENCE, not fluorescence: the stones charge in daylight and give it back after dark, so they can only be FOUND at night, by their own light, among identical grey gravel. This solves the hole in the earlier framing — a flood warning to villages safely up on benches threatened nobody, and neither 'villages beside the water' nor 'the water rises enormously' was plausible. The beacons do not mean flee. THEY MEAN DO NOT GO DOWN TONIGHT. The physics locks together: the same brilliant sun charges the stones AND swells the tarn, so **the best night to gather is the most dangerous night**, which is why the chain has to work at all. The gathering window is the pre-dawn low water (glacier-fed rivers run to a daily minimum in the small hours, after the afternoon melt pulse has passed), and that is exactly when a moraine failure would put a surge through the braids — lethal to anyone on the bars, barely touching the benches. Thematic rhyme worth protecting: the stones are invisible by day and obvious at night, exactly as the sightline network is invisible on paper and obvious once you have stood there. NAME IS PROVISIONAL — 'glimstone' follows the world's plain-compound toponymy (Fenwatch, Slatecrag, Thornbeck) and 'glim' is a genuine old word for a light. Alternatives if it grates: daystone, sunhold, the glim.

check.prompt: The ledgers from this watchpost are open on the desk: a count of every dispatch that passed between two stations of the network this season. Before anything else, see what the correspondence actually looks like. Which single link — one station writing to another — carries the most dispatches? Assign that link's row of the ledger to an object called answer, then click "Check my answer".
check.expr: local({ a <- answer; if (is.data.frame(a)) return(nrow(a) >= 1 && identical(as.character(a$origin[1]), "Anvil") && identical(as.character(a$destination[1]), "Ladder")); s <- tolower(paste(as.character(unlist(a)), collapse = " ")); i <- regexpr("anvil", s); j <- regexpr("ladder", s); i > 0 && j > 0 && i < j })
check.hint: Keep the one row of dispatch_ledger with the largest dispatches and assign it to answer — for example with arrange() and slice(), or filter() on the maximum.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: the heaviest link in the ledger is Anvil → Ladder, 2,604 dispatches — the forge writing to the fuel store.
wrong: Each row of the ledger is one link: a station writing to another, with how many dispatches went that way. Sort the rows by dispatches and keep the top one.
Mind the direction. Two stations writing to each other are two separate links, and only one of them is the heaviest.
You want the single row with the largest value in dispatches — not the station that turns up in the most rows.

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the flagged yard of a small stone signal station low on the valley floor — the viewer is standing IN the middle of the yard, ringed by its drystone wall, with the office range along one side and the whole range rising beyond. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is a plain drystone yard wall running level and unbroken, with the empty deep-cobalt sky and the far white peaks standing quietly above it: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, a plain drystone yard wall running level and unbroken with the empty deep-cobalt sky and the far white peaks above it, the left half of that one view, joining its other half cleanly at the seam directly behind you; to the left, a long sorting bench under a lean-to roof of slate, its pigeonholes stuffed with bundled correspondence tied in string, a franking stamp and a stack of flat wicker trays beside it; to the left of centre, beyond the low yard wall the braided river spread wide across its pale gravel bars, and lying along the whole length of the water a low band of dawn mist, waist-deep and luminous, breaking over the gravel plots, the drystone windbreaks and the line of wading stakes that marks the ford; dead ahead in the centre, the long stone office under its slate roof, its shutters propped open on a plain deal writing-desk where two heavy dispatch ledgers lie open side by side under a brass rule, with a stone inkwell, a tray of pens and a scuffed leather satchel beside them; across the office's slate roof lies a LARGE patch of old snow, covering a good third of the roof, soft, grey-white and visibly melting — thinning and slumped at its lower edge, with wet dark slates showing through where it has already gone and meltwater darkening the slates below it down to the gutter; just right of centre, the office chimney close at hand, putting up a broad soft plume of woodsmoke that rolls out low and heavy over the slates in the cold air, and far up the valley beyond it a single hair-thin thread of grey smoke standing quietly above the benches; to the right, a slate water butt against the yard wall with a wooden dipper hung on its rim, a mounting block, and a barrow of split kindling standing beside them; beyond it to the right, the yard gate standing open in the drystone wall, and beyond it the ridge path climbing away north-north-west out of the valley in a long series of grassy zigzags, gaining height fast; to the right, at the near corner of the office range a lead gutter runs off the slate roof and turns down into a stub spout directly above the slate water butt, and a heavy unbroken rope of snowmelt is pouring from that spout straight down into the butt, which is brim-full and slopping over its rim onto the cobbles, the water loud and fast with the warm week, pouring hard and unbroken, the butt brim-full and slopping over; on the far right, the same plain drystone yard wall running level and unbroken with the empty deep-cobalt sky and the far white peaks above it, the other half of that one view, joining cleanly at the seam directly behind you. brilliant hard high-altitude sun in a clear deep-cobalt sky, thin cold air and hard-edged shadows, blinding snow glare on the high tops; deep cobalt, blinding white snow and pale blue glacier ice, wet grey slate, bleached straw grass lit with a thin scatter of alpine flower colour, milk-jade meltwater, and one restrained note of rust-orange on iron; painterly, cinematic, subtle film grain, weathered and workmanlike; cold blue dawn shadow still filling the valley floor, frost in the lee of every wall, the sun already hard on the tops above. no flame or ember visible anywhere in the yard — the office chimney smokes but no fire is seen; no watchtower, beacon or signal tower anywhere in the view — this station carries no tower; no overcast and no flat grey cloud sheet — the sky overhead is clear, hard and deep cobalt, the only cloud is the low mist lying on the river; no flame, ember or lit fire anywhere — the iron fire-basket on this platform is cold and unlit; no OTHER watchtower, beacon, signal post, mast or built structure anywhere on the far ridges, shoulders or peaks — the viewer is standing on the only signal post in the view; no people; no lettering, captions, text, signage, numerals or UI; no glowing or luminous objects; no dusk, no golden hour and no amber light; no single symmetrical postcard peak centred in the frame and no travel-poster framing; nothing ruined, no rubble and no collapsed masonry — this is a kept, working signal service. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into a plain drystone yard wall running level and unbroken, with the empty deep-cobalt sky and the far white peaks standing quietly above it, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

pick.prompt: Stations write to each other in both directions, but not evenly, and the imbalance is worth knowing. Which station sends far more dispatches than it ever receives? Plot it, assign your plot to p, and click that station on your chart.
pick.plotCode:
sent <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(dispatch_ledger, station = origin), sent = sum(dispatches))
recv <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(dispatch_ledger, station = destination), received = sum(dispatches))
p <- ggplot(dplyr::left_join(sent, recv, by = "station"), aes(received, sent)) +
     geom_point()
pick.hint: One station sits far from the rest once sending is set against receiving — that is the lopsided one.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: Fenwatch sends 1,975 dispatches and receives only 202, nearly ten to one.
wrong: A station sends when it is the origin and receives when it is the destination. Total each separately for every station, then plot one against the other.
Busy is not the same as lopsided. A station that sends a great deal but receives about as much back is balanced — look for the one whose sending dwarfs its receiving.
Check the direction: you want the station that sends many times more than it receives, not one that receives more than it sends.

pick.prompt: Stations write to each other in both directions, but not evenly, and the imbalance is worth knowing. Which station sends far more dispatches than it ever receives? Plot it, assign your plot to p, and click that station on your chart.
pick.plotCode:
sent <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(dispatch_ledger, station = origin), sent = sum(dispatches))
recv <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(dispatch_ledger, station = destination), received = sum(dispatches))
p <- ggplot(dplyr::left_join(sent, recv, by = "station"), aes(received, sent)) +
     geom_point()
pick.hint: One station sits far from the rest once sending is set against receiving — that is the lopsided one.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: Fenwatch sends 1,975 dispatches and receives only 202, nearly ten to one.
wrong: A station sends when it is the origin and receives when it is the destination. Total each separately for every station, then plot one against the other.
Busy is not the same as lopsided. A station that sends a great deal but receives about as much back is balanced — look for the one whose sending dwarfs its receiving.
Check the direction: you want the station that sends many times more than it receives, not one that receives more than it sends.

pick.plotCode:
both <- dplyr::bind_rows(dplyr::transmute(dispatch_ledger, station = origin, dispatches),
                         dplyr::transmute(dispatch_ledger, station = destination, dispatches))
totals <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(both, station), total = sum(dispatches))
p <- ggplot(totals, aes(reorder(station, total), total)) +
     geom_col() +
     coord_flip() +
     labs(x = NULL, y = "Dispatches sent and received")

You want the station with the largest combined total of dispatches sent and received.

pick.prompt: The filed report in your hand blames the busiest station in the network for hoarding fire wood - the fuel the beacons use. Which watchstation is that? Counting everything a station sends and everything it receives, which station handles the most dispatches overall? Plot it, assign your plot to p, and click that station on your chart.
pick.plotCode:
both <- dplyr::bind_rows(dplyr::transmute(dispatch_ledger, station = origin, dispatches),
                         dplyr::transmute(dispatch_ledger, station = destination, dispatches))
totals <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(both, station), total = sum(dispatches))
p <- ggplot(totals, aes(reorder(station, total), total)) +
     geom_col() +
     coord_flip() +
     labs(x = NULL, y = "Dispatches sent and received")
pick.hint: One station's total stands clear of every other — the one the report blamed.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: the Crown is the busiest station, 8,075 dispatches sent and received, well clear of the Ladder's 6,789.
wrong: A station's traffic is what it sends (as origin) plus what it receives (as destination). Total both ends for every station, then plot one bar per station.
Counting only one end, or counting how many links a station has rather than how many dispatches they carry, gives a different ranking. Add up dispatches over both ends.
You want the station with the largest combined total of dispatches sent and received.

worldPlatePrompt: A world-bible establishing plate for the Harrows: a working frontier signal service above an inhabited high river valley, under an early unseasonal thaw. One frame holding the whole world's vocabulary — high white snowfields and a cracked blue-white glacier tongue filling the head of the valley, and below its snout a milky green tarn held back by a loose grey moraine wall, brim-full and seeping; meltwater running hard down into a wide BRAIDED RIVER of milk-jade channels and pale gravel islands; on those islands the marks of nightly work — cleared gravel plots, low drystone windbreaks, wicker baskets and drying racks, and a line of wading stakes marking the ford from bank to bar; broad U-shaped valley walls of pale grass, scree and dark slate; small stone villages of slate roof and drystone wall on flat benches a few hundred metres above the water, a thin early flush of alpine wildflowers through the bleached grass, sheep and long-haired goats grazing small and scattered on the far slopes; squat round dry-laid watchtowers high on the bare ridge shoulders, each with an open iron fire-basket on a stone platform and a timber fuel-store beside it, cords of split wood under a slate lintel with chalked tallies on the door; beside one, a shallow basket of DULL GREY-WHITE PEBBLES, ordinary and unremarkable in daylight; from a distant tower a single thin column of grey signal smoke standing straight and legible for miles; a brass spyglass on a wooden tripod, folded linen survey sheets, a leather satchel of ledgers; and on the highest summit a stone dispatch post with a rack of signal shutters. Light: brilliant high-altitude midday sun in a clear deep-blue sky, thin cold air, hard-edged shadows, snow glare on the tops — bright and high-key, not hazy and not overcast. Palette: deep cobalt sky, blinding white snow and pale blue glacier ice, wet grey slate, bleached straw grass with a thin scatter of flower colour, milk-jade meltwater, pale river gravel, one restrained note of rust-orange on iron. Painterly, cinematic, subtle film grain, weathered and workmanlike. No people, no glowing or luminous objects, no lettering, no captions, no text, no readable writing, no signage, no UI. Not a travel poster and not a tourist viewpoint: no single symmetrical postcard peak centred in frame, no golden-hour glow, no dusk, no amber.
coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster: the bold dark silhouette of a squat round stone watchtower on a bare ridge, against a clear deep-blue high-altitude sky, with one thin column of smoke rising straight from it; behind and above, the hard white silhouette of a snowfield and glacier; three tiny points of warm fire-light strung along the darker ridgeline far below. One high-contrast silhouette, iconic and uncluttered, minimal detail, strong negative space, single centred focal subject. Flat limited palette: deep cobalt, blinding white, deep slate blue-grey, one warm ember orange. Soft film grain, painterly but clean. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.
